notes.meaning: Jeremiah makes clear that this message did not start with him. It came straight from the LORD. God gave him both what to say and how to say it.

A covenant is a binding agreement. "This covenant" is the agreement God made with Israel through Moses, written in His law. Many think it points to the Book of the Law found in the temple in King Josiah's day. The command "listen" is plural, so God was speaking to His prophets together. They were to remind the people of the agreement and press it on them.

The curse comes from Deuteronomy 27:26, where Moses warned what would happen to anyone who broke the covenant. God first rescued Israel from Egypt, which He calls an "iron furnace." That picture shows how fierce and long their slavery was. Only then did He ask them to obey, and He gave them a kind promise: "You will be My people, and I will be your God."

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Cambridge Bible thinks the words "and do them" may have slipped into verse 4 by mistake from verse 6.

notes.meaning: God had sworn an oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to give their families a rich land. He kept His word, and the people still lived in that land "to this day." Jeremiah answers "Amen," which means "so be it." He echoes the people's Amen in Deuteronomy 27 and agrees that God's warnings are just. Matthew Henry compares the covenant to a lease: obedience was the rent, and God could take the land back if the rent went unpaid.

Jeremiah is sent on a preaching tour through every town of Judah and every street of Jerusalem. The message is simple: hear God's covenant and do it. Hearing alone is not enough, as James 1:22 also teaches. Everyone needed to know their duty, their blessings and their danger.

God says He warned them "again and again" from the Exodus until Jeremiah's day. The older wording says He was "rising early," a picture of how eagerly He worked to warn them. Still, each person followed their own stubborn heart. So the warnings written in the covenant came true. Matthew Henry notes that God keeps track of how often we have been warned.

A "conspiracy" is a secret plot. The people's turning from God was so widespread that it looked like a planned plot. King Josiah had cleared out idol worship, but after his death the people went back to it. Israel in the north and Judah in the south had often been enemies. Yet both joined in this one thing: breaking God's covenant.

Disaster is coming, and they will not escape it. They will cry to God, but He will not listen. The Geneva Notes explain that their cries would come from pain, not from true faith and repentance (turning away from sin). Wesley puts it this way: those who would not hear God in good times will not be heard in bad times.

In their trouble, the people will run to the idols they burned incense to. Those idols cannot save them at all. They cannot even help themselves, so they cannot help anyone else. Only God is a real help in trouble.

Judah had as many gods as it had towns, and Jerusalem had as many idol altars as it had streets. The idol is called "shame" because it was shameful and would bring shame on them. "Baal" means "lord." It was a common name used for many false gods.

God tells Jeremiah not to pray for the nation to be spared. Matthew Henry says this was mainly a warning to the people: they had gone so far that even the prayers of others would not help them. Calvin adds that Jeremiah could still pray for the faithful few and for the future of God's people. What he could not do was ask God to cancel the judgment.

"My beloved" means Judah, the people God loved and chose. They still came to His temple, but they also worshiped idols. "Consecrated meat" means the meat of their sacrifices, the offerings they brought to God. Their sacrifices could not protect them while their hearts were far from Him. Worship on the outside cannot save people who keep loving their sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars say the Hebrew of this verse is hard to read and may have been damaged when it was copied. Some fix it using the old Greek translation. The Cambridge Bible, for example, reads "fat pieces" of sacrifices.

notes.meaning: God had made His people like a healthy, fruitful olive tree. It was a picture of His free and tender love. But a tree that bears no fruit will be burned. Some read the "mighty roar" as thunder, with lightning setting the tree on fire. Others take it as the noise of the invading Babylonian army.

The LORD planted this tree, so He has the right to pull it up. Their beauty and strength came from God's kindness, not from themselves. By worshiping Baal they brought disaster on themselves. As Matthew Henry says, every sin against God is also a sin against ourselves.

Jeremiah now turns to a plot against his own life. He knew nothing about it until God showed it to him, so he could be on guard. He suddenly switches from "the LORD" to "You." That shows how deeply moved he was.

Jeremiah was like a tame pet lamb that trusts its family and has no idea it is being led to be killed. The plotters were people from his own hometown. "Destroy the tree with its fruit" means "kill the prophet and put an end to his message." Many Christians see here a picture of Jesus, rejected by His own people and called a lamb in Isaiah 53:7.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The old Latin Bible reads "let us put wood into his bread." Some early church writers, followed later by Catholic teachers, saw this as a picture of Christ's cross and His body.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah takes his case to God. God judges fairly and sees the deepest thoughts and feelings of the heart. Jeremiah leaves the matter in God's hands instead of getting even himself. Older writers say his wish to see God's justice came from zeal for God, not personal hatred. Some read his words as a prediction: "I will see Your vengeance." Matthew Henry adds that Jesus also taught us to pray for those who hurt us.

Anathoth was Jeremiah's hometown, a town where priests lived. Its people told him to stop speaking for God or they would kill him. They hated being corrected and wanted to be flattered. Their threat shows it was really God's message they rejected. Jesus later met the same treatment in His hometown of Nazareth.

God answers the plot Himself. The men of Anathoth will die by the sword and by hunger when the Babylonians invade. They wanted to wipe out Jeremiah and his name, so they themselves will have no survivors left. "The year of their punishment" means the time God has set to judge them.
